reason: The sources robustly support over a dozen cross-verified claims across independent sites detailing Sagittarius A*'s mass, light-speed orbital dynamics, imaging challenges, and violent past.
story: At the center of our Milky Way galaxy, 27,000 light-years away, lurks Sagittarius A*—a supermassive black hole packing four million times the mass of our Sun. While it seems quiet today, it is far from harmless. Gas in its accretion disk whips around at nearly the speed of light, completing full orbits in mere minutes. This extreme motion made imaging it an astronomical nightmare; when the Event Horizon Telescope linked observatories across Earth to photograph it, the swirling disk changed minute by minute, requiring five years of supercomputer calculations to resolve. Even more terrifying, this sleeping giant has a violent history. Space telescope observations revealed that roughly 350 years ago, Sagittarius A* suddenly erupted, blasting out one million times more energy than it does now. We know this because that ancient flash is still echoing off a nearby molecular gas cloud, proving our central black hole can wake up at any time.
angle: Just 350 years ago, the Milky Way's dormant supermassive black hole suddenly erupted with one million times more energy than it releases today, leaving an echoing X-ray reflection.

claims.claim: Sagittarius A* (abbreviated Sgr A*) is the supermassive black hole situated at the Galactic Center of the Milky Way.
Sagittarius A* contains an estimated mass of approximately four million times that of the Sun.
Sagittarius A* is located roughly 27,000 light-years away from Earth.
The black hole itself is completely invisible because its gravitational pull is so strong that even light cannot escape.
The light and radiation detected by astronomers emanate from hot gas and dust swirling within an accretion disk around the black hole.
On May 12, 2022, astronomers unveiled the first direct visual image of Sagittarius A*.
The image was captured by the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration using a worldwide network of radio observatories.
Sagittarius A* was only the second supermassive black hole ever directly imaged, following the 2019 release of Messier 87's black hole (M87*).
The radio telescope observations used to construct the first image of Sagittarius A* were recorded in 2017.
It took scientists five years of complex supercomputer analysis and calculations to process the 2017 raw data into a final image.
By combining signals from observatories around the globe, the Event Horizon Telescope functions as an Earth-sized virtual telescope.
Gas and matter in the immediate vicinity of Sagittarius A* move at velocities approaching the speed of light.
While gas takes days to weeks to orbit M87*, gas orbits Sagittarius A* in mere minutes, causing rapid brightness fluctuations that made it far harder to photograph.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating that Sagittarius A* is a supermassive compact object by tracking stellar orbits.
The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile served as a key facility in the Event Horizon Telescope network.
Approximately 350 years ago, Sagittarius A* was far more active, releasing roughly one million times more energy than it emits today.
The black hole's ancient outburst was discovered by observing gamma and X-rays reflecting off the nearby giant molecular cloud Sagittarius B2.
The accretion disk of Sagittarius A* undergoes persistent flaring activity and sudden brightness eruptions.
Sagittarius A* is enveloped by organized magnetic fields that closely resemble the magnetic geometry found around M87*.

disputed: Spin parameter and rotation speed: S1 lists conflicting measurements ranging from less than 0.1 to 0.90, S5 notes an estimate of about half maximum rate while stating rotation was unknown, and S7 mentions spin as a target of future study (attribute: 'estimates of its rotation speed range from moderate to near the speed of light').

Cosmic funnel metaphor: The framing that the black hole warps space into a 'cosmic funnel' appears in modern popular press for specific spin studies but is not corroborated across independent sources here (leave out).

Flare eruption mechanisms: S1 suggests flares may stem from breaking asteroids or magnetic reconnection, S2 posits magnetic reconnection and plasma turbulence, and S5 attributes them to relativistic orbiting hot spots (attribute: 'astrophysicists suspect magnetic reconnection or turbulent plasma waves').
Nature of the orbiting G2 object: Hypotheses range from a bare gas cloud to a shrouded binary star merger (leave out as secondary to the black hole's main story).
